notes:
HEALTH NOTES - Maya (10/16)

TOPIC 1: CONTRACEPTION (BC)
- BC = prevents pregnancy, NOT all prevent STIs
- only condoms (ext + int) also lower STI risk. big one!!
- effectiveness = 'perfect use' vs 'typical use' (typical = real life, ppl forget)
- Tiers:
  * Most effective (>99%): implant, IUD (hormonal + copper), lasts yrs. LARC = long-acting reversible contraception
  * Pretty good (~93-96%): pill (daily, same time), patch, ring, shot (every 3 mo)
  * Barrier: ext condom ~87% typical / 98% perfect; 
  * Least: withdrawal ~80% typical, fertility awareness
- Emergency contraception (EC) = backup, NOT regular BC, works best ASAP (w/in 72 hrs, some up to 5 days)
- Abstinence = 100% if consistent
- Ms O said: doctor/nurse can help choose, confidentiality rules vary by state?? (ask her)
- Dual protection = condom + another method

TOPIC 2: STIs
- STI = sexually transmitted infection (used to say STD)
- Bacterial: chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis -> curable w/ antibiotics
- Viral: HIV, HPV, herpes (HSV), hep B -> managed/not curable (HPV + hep B have vaccines!)
- Many have NO symptoms -> only testing tells you
- Untreated chlamydia/gonorrhea can -> PID, infertility
- Transmission: vaginal, anal, oral sex; skin-to-skin for HPV/herpes; also blood/mother to baby
- NOT spread by toilet seats, hugging, sharing food
- Prevention: abstinence, condoms every time, vaccines, testing, talking to partner
- Stigma = bad, getting tested is responsible

TO STUDY: effectiveness %s, curable vs not, QUIZ 3 sat 10/24!!! make flashcards

PUBERTY & HORM0NES - Ch. 7

Puberty = period when body matures & becomes capable of reproducfion. Begins ~ages 8-13 in girls, 9-14 in boys.

Hypothalamus signals the pituitary gland -> releases FSH and LH (gonadotropins).

Girls: ovaries make estrogen -> breast development, widening of hips, menstruai cycle begins (menarche)
Boys: testes make testosterone -> deeper voice, facial hair, [unreadable] growth, sperm production

Both: growth spurt, body odor, acne (oil glands), emotional changes/mood swings

Note: Timing varies a lot - being earlyor late is normaI and usually not a concem.

Key terms: hormone, gland, menarche, ovulafion
transcript:
Okay, so, um, good morning everybody, let's get settled. Today we're talking about contraception effectiveness, and, uh, this is where a lot of people get confused, so let's go slowly.

So first, the big idea. When we say a method is, you know, ninety-some percent effective, what does that actually mean? It means that if one hundred people use that method for a year, about that many will not get pregnant. So if a method is ninety-three percent effective, then around seven out of a hundred people would get pregnant in a year. Um, make sense? Okay.

Now there are two numbers you'll see. Perfect use, and typical use. Perfect use is, like, you do everything exactly right, every single time. Typical use is real life. Real life means people forget a pill, or the condom isn't put on correctly, or whatever. So typical use is usually lower, and for some methods it's a lot lower.

So let's go through the tiers. At the top, we have the implant and the IUD. These are, um, over ninety-nine percent effective, and the cool thing is, there's nothing to remember. Once it's in, it works for years. The difference between perfect and typical use is basically nothing. This will be on the exam, so write this down: the methods with the smallest gap between perfect and typical use are the implant and IUD, because they don't depend on you remembering anything.

Next tier, so, the pill, the patch, the ring, and the shot. Around ninety-three to ninety-six percent with typical use. The pill has to be taken every day at about the same time. The shot is every three months, so you have to, you know, show up for the appointment.

Then barrier methods. External condoms are about eighty-seven percent with typical use, but ninety-eight percent with perfect use. That's a big gap! And, um, condoms are the one method here that also lowers the risk of many STIs. So that's why we talk about dual protection, meaning using a condom plus another method.

And, sorry, totally off topic, did anyone see the game Friday? I cannot believe that last-second field goal. My neighbor was yelling so loud my dog hid under the couch. Okay, okay, back to it.

So emergency contraception. This is not a regular method. It's a backup, like if a condom breaks. It works best the sooner it's used. Some kinds work up to five days, but, um, earlier is better. And it doesn't end an existing pregnancy, that's a myth we should clear up.

And abstinence, which means choosing not to have sex, is the only method that's one hundred percent effective, as long as it's practiced consistently.

Oh, and an announcement. Quiz 3 on contraception was supposed to be this Saturday, October 24th, but I'm moving it to Thursday, October 29th, because a bunch of you have the band competition. So you get a few extra days. Same format, online, same topic.

For homework, um, make a chart comparing three methods: effectiveness, how often you use it, and whether it protects against STIs. Any questions? Yes, in the back? Good question, we'll cover that next class.
